title: Whenever We Remember You
hookLine: night three: the gods are offered any boon, and ask only that she come whenever they remember her
carry: remember the goddess, and she comes again

lines: THE ROOT OF A DAILY PRACTICE.
cards: Choose a boon. The path heard the goddess say it to the gods earlier this year, reading the Devi Mahatmya whole.

The buffalo demon is dead, and the gods could ask for anything: riches, safety forever, a share of her power. Tonight is night three, the last of the nights that, in one way of counting, belong to Durga.
And that old request, from the end of the fourth chapter, turns out to be the root of something Hindus do every day.

teach.b: Here's their answer, in paraphrase. Everything has already been done for us, they say, because our enemy is dead.
But if you'll give us a boon, then whenever we remember you again, destroy our worst troubles. And be gracious to anyone who praises you with these hymns. The goddess agrees, and vanishes.

Look at what they didn't ask for: not a fortress that would last forever, not a guarantee that nothing bad would happen again. As if they know it will. Heaven has been lost once; it can be lost twice.
So they ask for a promise of return: remember me, and I'll come.

That's a big teaching, and it has a name: smarana, remembering God. In Hindu devotion, calling the divine to mind, by name, by hymn, by a picture on the wall, isn't just thinking about her. It's how she's called.
That's why some families recite the Devi Mahatmya, the Chandi path, every Navaratri, and again in hard times: the reciting is the remembering the gods asked for.
It's why a grandmother says the goddess's name under her breath in a hospital corridor. Some devotees take the promise literally: in trouble, recite, and she comes.
Others read it inwardly: the remembering is itself the help, the moment a person turns toward something larger than the mess in front of them. And the circle is wide.

teach.h: FOR ANYONE WHO SINGS THESE HYMNS.
teach.b: The gods don't ask only for themselves, but for anyone who sings these hymns.
Three nights in, Durga's lesson is complete: she clears the road, she carries you across, and she comes again whenever she's remembered.

how: Some devotees recite chapters of the Devi Mahatmya during Navaratri, or in times of trouble, holding to the gods' boon in chapter four that the goddess will come when she is remembered.

games.q: what does “navaratri as a nine-night curriculum” mean?
o: a boon: whenever we remember you, come
a boon: a share of her power, so they'd never need her
a boon: a fortress no demon could ever enter

p: the goddess's offer to the gods

s: the gods ask the goddess for riches and lasting safety
they ask that she come whenever they remember her, and destroy their worst troubles.
the gods ask the boon for others too
for anyone who praises her with these hymns.
the clearing nights promise a road that stays clear for good
the road fills up again; what the first nights teach is a way of returning.

games.q: it's night three, and the clearing nights are ending. the road will fill up again. what does the gods' boon suggest you carry into the next nights?
o: a promise that nothing will block the road again.
a way of returning: something to remember when it fills up.
a plan to stop clearing altogether.
games.why: the gods don't ask for a road that stays clear. they ask that whenever they remember her, she destroy their worst troubles: a way of returning.

practice: Choose one name for the divine you'd want to remember in a hard moment: Durga, Ma, Ram, or the name you use. Say it once, quietly, and let the silence after it be long.
Then picture one place this week where you'll need it, a waiting room, a test, a hard call, and say it once more, as if you were already there.
If you don't pray, choose one word that steadies you and practice returning to it the same way.

wordCard.voice: Navaratri, night three. The close of Durga's nights, with the gods' boon: whenever we remember you, come. Smarana, remembering, is how she's called.

orig.note: Sanskrit vara: a boon, a gift chosen by the one who receives it.

carryVoice: Your line: remember the goddess, and she comes again. The gods asked for a way back, not a fortress. Three nights in.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya 4 (closing verses: the boon asked by the gods)
